cards.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
cards.content:
Understanding the difference between concurrency and parallelism is fundamental for a Java Developer:

  • Concurrency: About copinement/structure. It is the ability to run multiple tasks out-of-order or in interleaved fashion on a single core.
  • Parallelism: About execution. It is the ability to run multiple tasks at the exact same time on multiple processing cores.

cards.title: Creating Threads in Java
cards.content:
In Java, there are two primary ways to define and execute a thread:

  1. Extending the Thread class.
  2. Implementing the Runnable interface (preferred for separation of concerns).
// Using Runnable lambda syntax
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("Running in: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
Thread thread = new Thread(task);
thread.start();

cards.title: The Thread Lifecycle
cards.content:
A Java thread can exist in one of the following states defined by the Thread.State enum:

  • NEW: Created but not yet started.
  • RUNNABLE: Executing in the JVM (or waiting for OS resource allocation).
  • BLOCKED: Waiting to acquire a monitor lock.
  • WAITING: Waiting indefinitely for another thread to perform an action.
  • TIMED_WAITING: Waiting for a specified period.
  • TERMINATED: Finished execution.

cards.title: Race Conditions & Data Races
cards.content:
A race condition occurs when the program's outcome depends on the unpredictable sequence or timing of thread execution.

A data race happens when two or more threads concurrently access the same memory location, at least one of these accesses is a write, and there is no synchronization coordinating them.

cards.title: The synchronized Keyword
cards.content:
Java provides built-in lock mechanisms via the synchronized keyword. It ensures that only one thread can execute a block of code or a method on a locked monitor object at a time.

public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;
    
    public synchronized void increment() {
        count++; // Thread-safe operation
    }
}

cards.title: The volatile Keyword
cards.content:
The volatile keyword solves visibility issues rather than atomicity. It ensures that reads and writes to a variable go directly to the main memory, bypassing CPU caches.

Use volatile when you have a flag checked by one thread and updated by another, but avoid using it for compound operations like incrementing (i++).

cards.title: The Executor Framework
cards.content:
Manually managing individual threads is highly discouraged in production Java. Instead, use the ExecutorService API.

ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);

executor.submit(() -> {
    System.out.println("Task executed inside thread pool");
});

executor.shutdown();

content.instruction: Order the lifecycle actions of an ExecutorService correctly from instantiation to complete shutdown:

items.text: Create an ExecutorService instance via Executors factory.
Submit Callable or Runnable tasks to the pool.
Invoke shutdown() to stop accepting new tasks.
Invoke awaitTermination() to block until active tasks complete execution.

cards.title: CompletableFuture (Asynchronous Programming)
cards.content:
Introduced in Java 8, CompletableFuture implements Future and CompletionStage, allowing you to write non-blocking asynchronous pipeline structures.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Hello")
    .thenApply(val -> val + " World")
    .thenAccept(System.out::println);
